title: Cultural Variance
hook: Whether faces speak one human language has divided science for a century, and the honest answer changes what you are allowed to assume.
why:
Every reader of people eventually meets the question at the centre of this chapter. When someone from a culture you do not know smiles, frowns or gasps, can you trust your reading of it? If human expressions are a universal language, much of what you have learned travels with you. If they are local dialects, much of it does not.

Scientists have argued about this for a hundred and fifty years, and the argument is not settled. This chapter lays out the evidence on both sides honestly: Darwin's original question, the studies that seemed to prove universality, the critiques that showed how much depended on how the question was asked, the newer research suggesting that different cultures carry different mental pictures of the same emotion, the evidence from voices and from millions of videos, and the idea of dialects that tries to reconcile them. It ends with what a careful reader is entitled to assume. The practical method for working in an unfamiliar culture is in Part VI; this chapter gives you the science that method rests on.

teach.p:
In 1872 Charles Darwin published *The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals*. Part of his evidence came from a questionnaire he sent to missionaries, colonial officials and travellers around the world, asking whether the people they lived among showed astonishment with raised eyebrows and an open mouth, shame with a blush, contempt with a raised lip, and so on. The replies, filtered through the assumptions of the people writing them, mostly said yes. Darwin concluded that many expressions were inherited and shared by all humans.

For much of the twentieth century, social scientists leaned the other way. Anthropologists such as Margaret Mead and Ray Birdwhistell emphasised how much expression differed from one culture to another, and Birdwhistell argued that there were no universal expressions at all, only learned conventions as varied as languages. The smile, he suggested, meant different things in different places, and in some places very little.

Both positions were built on limited evidence. Darwin's correspondents saw what they expected. The relativists relied heavily on striking anecdotes and on the idea, popular at the time, that almost everything human was learned.

The question matters for a reader because it determines how far your experience transfers. If expressions are universal, your years of reading faces at home give you a head start anywhere. If they are local, they may give you a head start in the wrong direction, as the chapter on cross-cultural calibration in Part VI warned.

Keep the question open as you read. The honest answer turns out to be neither of the two that were first proposed.
teach.disconfirm: If the question of universality had been settled decisively in one direction, this chapter would be unnecessary. The fact that careful researchers still disagree, using better methods than Darwin had, is itself the main reason for caution.

teach.p:
In the late 1960s Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen set out to test universality in a place where people had had very little contact with outsiders or their media. Among the Fore people of the highlands of Papua New Guinea, they told short stories, such as *her child has died*, and asked people to choose which of several photographs of faces matched the story. Published in 1971, the results showed agreement well above chance for most emotions, though fear and surprise were often confused with each other. When Fore people were asked to show how they would look in each story, Americans shown photographs of their faces could identify many of the intended emotions.

In 1987 Ekman and colleagues extended the work to ten cultures and again found substantial agreement about which emotion the classic faces showed. Studies of spontaneous expression added weight. In 2009 David Matsumoto and Bob Willingham compared the faces of sighted and congenitally blind judo athletes after winning and losing matches and found that the blind athletes produced the same facial expressions, though they had never seen a face. The chapter on the spine as status described a similar finding for pride and shame postures.

These results persuaded much of the field that a small number of basic emotions, such as happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise and disgust, have universal facial expressions rooted in biology, which cultures then regulate through display rules. This view shaped decades of research, training and technology, including the emotion-reading software discussed in Part VI.

The evidence for some shared core is real. The question is how large the core is, and how much the methods inflated it.
teach.disconfirm: If people in remote cultures, matching faces to stories, had performed at chance for every emotion, the universal view would have failed at its first test. They did better than chance for most emotions, which is why the view was taken seriously.

teach.h: The case against: how the question was asked.
teach.p:
In 1994 James Russell published a long critique of the universality studies. He did not argue that faces mean nothing across cultures. He argued that the methods used had made agreement look much stronger than it was.

Most studies gave people a short list of emotion words or stories and asked them to choose one for each face. That forced choice, Russell pointed out, lets people succeed by elimination: if you know one face is happy and one sad, the remaining choices are easier. The faces were posed, exaggerated prototypes rather than expressions seen in daily life. Many participants had some exposure to Western media. And agreement fell, sometimes sharply, as samples became more remote and methods less constrained.

A study published in 2014 by Maria Gendron, Debi Roberson, Marietta van der Vyver and Lisa Feldman Barrett tested this directly. They asked Himba participants in a remote part of Namibia to sort photographs of posed faces into piles, freely, without any emotion words being provided. The Himba did not produce the six Western categories. They tended to group smiling faces together, and often sorted the others by what the person seemed to be doing, *laughing*, *looking at something*, rather than by an inner feeling. Supplying emotion words changed their sorting somewhat, but still did not produce the Western six.

The lesson is not that faces are meaningless. It is that how much meaning they seem to carry across cultures depends heavily on how you ask, and that people in many places may read a face first as an action in a situation, not as a window onto a feeling.

The answer you get depends a great deal on the question you ask.
teach.disconfirm: If people in remote cultures sorted faces freely into the same six groups that Western participants produce, the method critique would lose most of its force. The free-sorting studies have so far found otherwise, though they are few and debated.

teach.h: Different cultures carry different pictures of a feeling.
teach.p:
In 2012 Rachael Jack, Philippe Schyns and colleagues used a clever method to find out what people in different cultures expect an emotional face to look like. They showed participants thousands of computer-generated faces with random combinations of facial movements and asked them, each time, which emotion the face showed, if any. From the answers they reconstructed each participant's mental picture of each emotion.

Western participants' pictures fell into six fairly distinct groups resembling the classic prototypes. East Asian participants' pictures overlapped more, and they relied more on the eyes than the mouth to represent the intensity of a feeling. The researchers concluded that the six classic faces are not equally shared, and that different cultures carry different expectations about which parts of the face carry an emotion.

A study in the Trobriand Islands of Papua New Guinea, published in 2016 by Carlos Crivelli, James Russell and colleagues, found something even more striking. The wide-eyed, gasping face that Western research treats as the prototype of fear was read by Trobriand Islanders as a threatening display, closer to anger, the kind of face used to intimidate. The same configuration carried something like the opposite meaning.

For a reader, these findings mean that fine distinctions between expressions are the least likely to travel. Telling fear from surprise, or contempt from disgust, by face alone is unreliable even at home, and across cultures it may be wrong in ways you cannot detect. Where in a face to look for intensity, eyes or mouth, may also differ.
teach.disconfirm: If mental pictures of emotional faces turned out to be the same in every culture tested, the dialect view would be unnecessary. The reverse correlation and Trobriand studies found real differences, though both await wider replication.
teach.pullQuote: The same face can carry something close to the opposite meaning in another place.

teach.p:
Faces are not the only evidence. In 2010 Disa Sauter, Frank Eisner, Paul Ekman and Sophie Scott played recordings of nonverbal vocalisations, such as laughs, screams, sighs and sobs, to Himba listeners and to English listeners, and asked them to match each sound to a short emotional story. Both groups recognised several basic emotions in the other group's sounds at above chance. Laughter was recognised especially well across the two cultures; some other positive sounds were recognised mainly within a culture. The chapter on reading the room described a related finding: listeners in twenty-four societies could hear whether people laughing together were friends.

A very different kind of evidence came in 2021, when Alan Cowen, Dacher Keltner and colleagues used machine learning to analyse facial expressions in about six million videos from 144 countries, along with the situations in which they appeared: weddings, sporting events, protests, funerals, fireworks and so on. They found that about sixteen kinds of expression were associated with similar kinds of situation in every region of the world they studied, with roughly seventy percent of the pattern shared across regions. The method depends on how the algorithms were trained, and it measures what faces go with what situations rather than what people feel.

Taken together, these findings suggest that some links between expressions and situations are widely shared, especially for laughter and for expressions in strongly patterned situations such as celebrations and grief. They do not settle how people read each other's faces in ordinary conversation, where situations are subtler and expressions faint.

Shared contexts are a better guide across cultures than shared faces.
teach.disconfirm: If vocalisations such as laughter and screams were recognised only within cultures, never across them, the case for a shared core would be much weaker. The cross-cultural vocal studies found otherwise, especially for laughter.

teach.h: Dialects: one language with strong accents.
teach.p:
Hillary Anger Elfenbein has offered a way of holding these findings together, which she calls dialect theory. Emotional expression, on this view, is like a language spoken in many dialects. There is a shared core, a broad family resemblance between how people everywhere express some feelings, especially in strong and clear situations. On top of the core, each culture develops its own accents: particular movements it uses more or less, particular ways of combining them, particular meanings for configurations that elsewhere mean something else.

Dialect theory explains several findings at once. It explains why recognition across cultures is above chance but lower than within a culture, the in-group advantage described in Part VI. It explains why people who live among another culture for some time become better at reading it: they learn the accent. And it explains why some expressions, like laughter, travel well, while others, like the gasping face, can be read in very different ways.

The dialect view also fits what this book has said about individuals. Within any culture, people have their own idiolects: a colleague whose resting face looks stern, a friend who laughs when anxious, a father who goes silent when moved. A reader always has to learn the local accent and the personal one.

For practical purposes, think of what you already know about faces as a native speaker's knowledge of one dialect. It will help you understand the rough sense of much that you see elsewhere, and it will mislead you about the details.
teach.disconfirm: If people who spent long periods in another culture became no better at reading its expressions over time, the idea of learnable accents would be weak. Studies of exposure and recognition, and the experience of most long-term migrants, suggest that they do improve.

teach.h: What you are allowed to assume.
teach.p:
From all this, a few working rules follow, and they apply in your own culture as much as in any other.

You may assume, weakly, that some links are widely shared: smiling and laughing in pleasant and sociable situations, crying in grief, the expanded and slumped postures of victory and defeat. Even these carry local accents. A smile may be embarrassment, apology or politeness as easily as pleasure, and in some places it is used much more freely with strangers than in others.

You should not assume that fine distinctions travel: fear from surprise, contempt from disgust, worry from concentration. Nor should you assume that intensity is shown in the same part of the face, or that a configuration you know carries the meaning you know. When the stakes matter, treat any reading of an unfamiliar face as a description of movement in a situation, and ask.

You should assume that context carries more of the meaning than the face does, everywhere. The chapter on the face showed this even within one culture. Across cultures, the situation, the relationship and the local norms carry still more.

And you should assume that your informants, the people who know both their culture and yours, are worth more than any finding in this chapter. The method in Part VI, building local baselines and asking people who know, exists because the science described here gives you a rough map and not the ground.

A shared core, strong accents, and context deciding most of the meaning: that is the honest answer, and it is enough to work with.
teach.disconfirm: If careful readers who relied on the classic faces in unfamiliar cultures turned out to be as accurate as those who relied on context and local informants, the rules in this block would be too cautious. The evidence described here suggests they would not.

poseGallery.doCaption: Holding them as a rough shared core, with local accents.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Assuming the textbook faces mean the same everywhere.
poseGallery.annotation: Universality studies found above-chance agreement, but the methods inflated it. Fine distinctions are the least likely to travel.

poseGallery.doCaption: Asking what that face means here.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Reading a gasping face as fear in every culture.
poseGallery.annotation: In the Trobriand Islands the classic fear face read as a threat display. A configuration can carry very different meanings in different places.

poseGallery.doCaption: Learning where people here show intensity.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Watching only the mouth for feeling, as at home.
poseGallery.annotation: Different cultures carry different pictures of a feeling, and some rely more on the eyes. Your habits of attention are part of your dialect.

poseGallery.doCaption: Trusting smiles and laughter a little, and checking the rest.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Dismissing all shared expression as myth.
poseGallery.annotation: There is a shared core, especially for laughter and strong situations. The honest position lies between the two extremes.

poseGallery.doCaption: Asking how your face reads here
poseGallery.dontCaption: Treating your own expressions as neutral
poseGallery.annotation: Your face speaks a dialect too. Across cultures, ask how your habits are read, and explain them aloud where they might mislead.

poseGallery.doCaption: Asking an informant what you are missing
poseGallery.dontCaption: Giving up on reading unfamiliar faces
poseGallery.annotation: When readings keep failing, do not withdraw. Ask someone who knows both dialects, and ask people directly when it matters.

caseStudy:
Ben, thirty-three, has taught English in Britain for eight years and moves to a language school in Seoul. He considers himself good at reading a classroom: he can tell from faces who is lost and who is bored. In his first month in Seoul his confidence goes. When he asks whether students have understood, many keep a calm, neutral face and nod, and then cannot do the exercise. Some smile when they get an answer wrong, which at home he would have read as not taking it seriously.

He asks a Korean colleague, Ji-woo, who taught in Australia for three years. She explains that some students, especially in front of a teacher, keep a composed face when confused, because showing confusion openly can feel like a loss of face for them or a criticism of the teacher. The smile at a wrong answer is often embarrassment, not amusement. Then she adds a caution: this is not true of every student, and the younger ones and those who have studied abroad are often quite different. She also tells him, kindly, that some students find his very expressive face a little overwhelming.

Ben changes his method. He stops relying on faces to check understanding and uses short written tasks instead. He watches for changes in each student's own baseline rather than reading their faces against his British classroom. He learns that one student, Min-jun, presses his lips together briefly when lost, and another, Seo-yeon, goes very still. He tones down his own expressions a little.

By the end of the term his students are asking more questions. When one smiles at a wrong answer, he no longer reads it as carelessness. He reads it as a smile, in a situation, from a particular person, and asks.
observe: Watch a film or programme made in a culture you know little about, and note one expression whose meaning you were unsure of, and what the situation suggested.
Notice one occasion when someone smiled in a situation where you would not expect a smile, and list what else the smile might have meant.
Ask someone who has lived in two cultures which expressions they had to relearn, and note their answer.

drills.name: Movement and Situation
steps: Choose a clip from a film or documentary set in a culture you know little about.
Pause at three moments when a face changes, and describe each movement without naming an emotion.
Note the situation at each moment: who is present, what has just happened.
Write your first reading of each face, and then a reading based on the situation alone.
Note where the two readings differ.
variations: Repeat with a clip from a culture you know well, and compare how much the situation added there.
Try the exercise with the sound off, then with it on, and note how much of your reading the voice changed.
Watch the same scene twice, a week apart, and see whether your readings of each face have changed.

drills.name: Your Own Dialect
steps: List five expressions you use often, such as a particular smile, frown or way of showing surprise.
For each, write what you mean by it.
Ask someone from a different background, if you can, what each would mean to them.
Mark any where the meanings differ.
Write one sentence about which of your expressions might mislead people elsewhere.
variations: Ask a close friend from your own background the same questions, and see whether your expressions are as clear to them as you think.
Add one gesture or head movement to the list of five, and check its meaning in the same way.

drills.name: Informant Questions
steps: Find someone who has lived for some time in two cultures.
Ask which facial expressions or gestures they had to relearn when they moved.
Ask for a specific situation in which they were misread, or misread someone else.
Ask how long it took to feel at home reading people in the new culture.
Write down the answers as close to their words as you can.
variations: Ask your informant what they had to unlearn when they returned home, if they did.
Ask about one specific feeling, such as embarrassment, and how it is shown differently in each culture they know.

drills.name: Fine Distinctions
steps: Open the face plates of the six posed prototypes in the pose library.
Cover the labels and try to name each face.
Note which pairs you find hardest to tell apart.
Write down a situation in which each hard pair might occur.
Note how much easier the situation makes the distinction.
variations: Repeat with photographs of real, unposed faces from news or sports images, and compare the difficulty.
Ask a friend from another culture to do the same exercise, and compare which pairs each of you found hardest.

drills.name: Assumptions Audit
steps: Write down three readings of other people's faces you have made recently.
For each, mark whether it relied on a broad link, such as a smile in a pleasant moment, or a fine distinction, such as fear versus surprise.
For each fine distinction, write what in the situation supported it.
Mark any reading that relied on the face alone.
Write how you would check those readings next time.
variations: Repeat the audit for readings of people from your own culture, and compare how often you relied on the face alone.
Pick one person you work with from a different background and note, over a week, which of your readings of them you later confirmed.

quiz.q: What does the evidence best support about facial expressions across cultures?
options: They are a universal language and are read the same way everywhere
They are entirely learned and carry no shared meaning across cultures
There is a rough shared core, with strong local accents and context
Only Western faces show emotion clearly enough to be read by others
quiz.explain: Agreement across cultures is above chance, especially for laughter and strong situations, but methods inflated early estimates and some configurations carry different meanings elsewhere. Context does much of the work everywhere.

quiz.q: In Ekman and Friesen's study among the Fore of Papua New Guinea, what were participants asked to do?
options: Match photographs of faces to short stories about emotional situations
Pose a series of faces while being filmed by the visiting research team
Sort a pile of photographs freely into groups of their own choosing
Name the emotion shown in each face using a list of English words
quiz.explain: Participants chose which face matched a story, and did better than chance for most emotions, though fear and surprise were often confused. Critics later pointed out that this kind of forced choice can inflate agreement.

quiz.q: When Himba participants sorted photographs of faces freely, without being given emotion words, what happened?
options: They sorted them neatly into the same six groups Western participants use
They declined to sort the photographs at all, finding the task meaningless
They sorted the photographs only by the apparent age and sex of each person shown
They did not produce the six groups, often sorting faces by actions instead
quiz.explain: Smiling faces tended to go together, but other faces were often grouped by what the person seemed to be doing, such as laughing or looking. How much meaning faces seem to carry depends on how the question is asked.

quiz.q: Working abroad, you see a colleague make a wide-eyed, open-mouthed face that at home would mean fear. What fits this chapter?
options: Read it as fear, since the fear face has been shown to be universal
Treat it as a movement, and ask what it means here before concluding
Ignore it, since you cannot read faces at all in another culture
Mirror the expression back to show that you understand the feeling
quiz.explain: Fine distinctions travel least well, and in at least one society this very face reads as a threat display. Describing the movement and asking, the colleague or a local informant, avoids a confident misreading.

quiz.q: What did Crivelli and colleagues find about the wide-eyed gasping face in the Trobriand Islands?
options: It was read as fear, exactly as in Western studies of the face
It was not recognised as meaning anything in particular at all
It was read as a threatening display, closer to anger than to fear
It was read as surprise by adults and as fear by younger children
quiz.explain: The configuration Western research treats as the prototype of fear carried something close to the opposite meaning there. The same face can mean different things in different places.

quiz.q: A friend says research proves that emotions are universal, so he can read anyone, anywhere. What fits this chapter?
options: The core is rough, the accents are strong, and context decides most
He is right, since the universal faces have been shown in many studies
He is wrong, since research shows faces mean nothing across cultures
He is right about faces but wrong about voices, which are all learned
quiz.explain: Both extremes are unsupported. A shared core exists, especially for laughter and strong situations, but fine distinctions and many meanings are local, and context carries much of the meaning everywhere.

quiz.q: What did Elfenbein and Ambady find when they combined many studies of emotion recognition across cultures?
options: People recognised emotions equally well in members of every culture, without exception
People recognised emotions more accurately in their own group, an advantage that shrank with contact
People recognised emotions better in other cultures than their own, since they paid more attention
People could not recognise any emotions outside their own culture, even after long exposure
quiz.explain: The in-group advantage means people read their own group a little more accurately, and the advantage shrinks where groups have more contact. Reading another dialect is a skill that improves with exposure.

quiz.q: An elderly patient from a culture that prizes composure shows a calm face and reports a low pain score, but has not moved her leg or eaten all day. What fits this chapter best?
options: Trust the calm face and the low score, since both point clearly to mild pain
Assume she is exaggerating her difficulty, since her face shows no sign of pain
Weigh her behaviour and her family's account more heavily than her calm face
Wait until she shows pain on her face before changing anything about her care
quiz.explain: Display rules shape how much pain people show, especially to strangers and doctors. Behaviour, such as not moving or eating, and the account of people who know her, carry more information than a face speaking an unfamiliar dialect.

quiz.q: A colleague says that because faces vary across cultures, nothing can be read from anyone's face abroad. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, since the evidence shows that facial expressions have no shared meaning at all
He is right about faces, though gestures such as the thumbs-up mean the same everywhere
He is wrong, since the evidence shows that all facial expressions are completely universal
Some broad links travel, such as smiles in pleasant situations, but fine distinctions need checking
quiz.explain: Dialect theory holds both truths: a shared core, especially for strong and clear situations, with local accents on top. Radical relativism is as much a failure as overconfident universalism.

quiz.q: According to research by Sauter and colleagues with Himba and English listeners, which kind of signal was recognised especially well across the two cultures?
options: Laughter, among nonverbal vocal sounds, was recognised especially well across the cultures
Facial expressions of disgust, which both groups matched to stories with near-perfect accuracy
Hand gestures for agreement and refusal, which turned out to be identical in both cultures
Silences of different lengths, which both groups used to signal the very same emotions
quiz.explain: Several basic emotions were recognised in the other group's vocal sounds at above chance, and laughter especially well. Voices may travel across cultures somewhat better than faces do.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific time when you read the face of someone from a background different from yours, and later learned you had been wrong, or suspected you might have been. Describe the movement you saw and the situation. Was your reading a broad one, such as pleasure or distress, or a fine distinction? What would the situation alone have told you? Knowing what this chapter says about shared cores and local accents, what would you now assume, and what would you ask?
reflection.guidance: The background need not be national; class, region, generation and religion carry their own dialects. Many people find that their misreading involved a fine distinction, or a smile in an unexpected place. The useful part is the last question: separating what you may reasonably assume from what you need to check.

failureMode: There are two opposite failures. The first is universalism: assuming that the classic faces mean the same everywhere, and reading people from other cultures with the confidence of a native speaker of a dialect that is not theirs. The second is radical relativism: deciding that because faces vary, nothing can be read across cultures at all, and withdrawing from people whose expressions are unfamiliar. A third failure is to swap one stereotype for another, learning that a culture is reserved or expressive and reading every person in it that way. And a fourth is to forget that the same lessons apply at home, where fine distinctions are unreliable and context carries most of the meaning. Assume a rough shared core, expect strong accents, trust context, and ask.

moreCases.title: The patient who did not show her pain
moreCases.scene:
Halima, eighty-one, is admitted to a hospital ward in Birmingham after a fall. She came to Britain from Somalia thirty years ago and speaks
  limited English. When the junior doctor, Tom, examines her hip, her face stays calm. She does not grimace, cry out or pull away; she looks at
  the ceiling and breathes slowly. When the interpreter asks about pain on a scale of nought to ten, she says three. Tom writes her up for mild
  pain relief.

  Her granddaughter, Amina, arrives that evening and is alarmed. She tells the nurse that her grandmother would never show pain in front of a
  stranger, let alone a young man, and that saying three to a doctor means it is bad. She points out that her grandmother has not eaten, has not
  moved her leg at all since she arrived, and has been gripping the bed rail all afternoon. The nurse calls Tom back. An X-ray the next morning
  shows a fractured hip.

Amina says afterwards that she has had to do this for her grandmother before, at a GP surgery and at a dentist. Each time, she says, the staff were kind, and each time they believed the calm face over everything else.

Later, on the ward round, the consultant asks Tom why he had judged the pain as mild. Tom says, honestly, that she looked comfortable and gave a low score. The consultant does not criticise him. She tells him that she made the same mistake early in her career, with a patient she still remembers, and asks him what he would look at next time.
moreCases.misread:
Tom read Halima's calm face as a sign of mild pain, through the dialect of expression he had grown up with, in which people in serious pain usually show it. He also took her number at face value, without considering what a number means to someone for whom complaining to a doctor is itself a kind of disrespect.

The misreading was not careless. Tom was busy, kind and following his training. His training had simply assumed a dialect of pain that Halima did not speak.

There was a second, quieter error. Tom treated the interpreter's translation of the number as the whole of the answer. He did not ask how Halima said it, whether she hesitated, or whether she added anything the interpreter left out as unimportant. An interpreter can carry words across a gap far more easily than a tone or a pause.
moreCases.betterRead:
Display rules, the norms about who may show what to whom, vary across cultures, generations, genders and settings, and pain is one of the feelings most shaped by them. Many older people, and people from cultures that prize composure, show very little pain on their faces, especially before strangers, doctors and men. A careful reader in Tom's position weighs the face least and the body and behaviour most: not moving the leg, not eating, gripping the rail. He asks the family what this person is like when they are hurting. And he treats a low pain score from someone likely to understate it as a reason to look harder, not to look away. The face was not lying. It was speaking a dialect Tom did not know.

Many hospitals now train staff in exactly this, and use pain assessment that relies on behaviour as well as self-report, particularly for older patients and those who do not share the clinician's language.

Tom, for his part, now asks families the same question on every admission: how does she usually show that she is hurting?

moreCases.title: Laughter at the bad news
moreCases.scene:
Graham, a British project manager, is on a video call with his counterpart in Osaka, Mr Takahashi, about a shipment that has been delayed by
  three weeks, which will cost Graham's company a good deal of money. Graham explains the problem carefully and seriously. Mr Takahashi listens,
  nods, and then laughs, a short, quiet laugh, before saying that this is very difficult and he is very sorry. He laughs again, briefly, when Graham
  mentions the penalty clause.

  Graham is furious. He tells his director afterwards that the Japanese side clearly does not take the delay seriously and is laughing at them. His
  director, who worked in Tokyo for four years, tells him that he has probably misread the laugh completely.

Graham's director also points out that Mr Takahashi had stayed on the call for an extra twenty minutes, which is not what someone indifferent to a problem does.

The delay itself was not Mr Takahashi's fault. A supplier further down the chain had failed an inspection, and his firm had found out only two days before the call. Graham knows this, but he had expected some visible sign of how seriously the other side took it: a grave expression, a long apology, perhaps an offer of compensation on the spot. Instead, as he saw it, he got two laughs.

He replays the moment several times on the recording. Each time, the laugh looks worse to him. He drafts an angry email to Mr Takahashi's manager, copying in his own director, and holds back from sending it only because his director asks to speak to him first.
moreCases.misread:
Graham read the laugh through his own dialect, in which laughing at someone else's bad news signals amusement, indifference or contempt. He did not consider that a laugh might mean something else in a different culture, or in a moment of shared embarrassment.

He then passed his reading on to his director as a fact about the other company, which, if his director had believed it, could have soured a long relationship over a laugh.

Graham also read the laugh in isolation. He took one sound from a forty-minute call and let it outweigh everything else that happened, including two apologies and a practical offer of help. That is the single-signal error from earlier chapters, made worse by an unfamiliar dialect.
moreCases.betterRead:
In many settings, including some in Japan, a short laugh can signal embarrassment, discomfort or an attempt to soften an awkward moment, rather than amusement. Laughter in general travels well across cultures, as Sauter and colleagues found, but particular uses of it do not. Graham's director suggested reading the rest of the call rather than the laugh: Mr Takahashi had apologised twice, offered to check alternative routes, and agreed to a follow-up call the next day. Those are the actions of a man taking a problem seriously. The laugh was the sound of a difficult moment, in a dialect Graham had not yet learned.

It is also worth noting that Graham's anger, visible on camera, will have been read through Mr Takahashi's dialect too, and may have increased the embarrassment that the laugh was trying to soften.

The director also advised Graham to say plainly, at the start of the follow-up call, how serious the delay was for his company, rather than hoping his face would carry the message. Words cross a cultural gap better than faces do.

moreCases.title: The engineer who did not smile at clients
moreCases.scene:
Mikko, a Finnish engineer, moves to his firm's office in Texas to lead a team that installs industrial equipment. He is highly respected at
  home for his calm and his competence. In Texas, his first two client meetings go badly. The clients find him cold and hard to read; one asks his
  manager afterwards whether Mikko is unhappy with the contract. Mikko is baffled. He thought the meetings went well. He listened carefully, answered
  every question precisely, and did not waste anyone's time with small talk.

  His American colleague, Jess, who sat in on both meetings, tells him that he did not smile once, that he barely nodded, and that he let silences
  run long after the clients spoke. To the clients, used to warm greetings and frequent smiles, this felt like disapproval. Mikko tells her that in
  Finland, smiling at strangers for no reason can seem insincere, and that silence after someone speaks is a sign that you are taking them seriously.

Mikko also mentions that he had found the clients' constant smiles slightly unnerving, and had wondered whether they were hiding their real view of the contract. The misreading, in other words, ran in both directions.

Mikko is not new to working abroad. He has spent time on projects in Germany and Sweden, where his manner caused no trouble at all, and he had assumed that professional behaviour was much the same everywhere. What troubles him most is that the clients' complaint feels like a complaint about his character rather than his work, and he does not know which part of himself he is supposed to change.
moreCases.misread:
The clients read Mikko's composed face and long silences as coldness and displeasure, through a dialect in which warmth is shown constantly and silence is uncomfortable. Mikko, in turn, read his own behaviour as respectful, through a dialect in which restraint is a courtesy. Each was reading accurately in their own language and wrongly across the gap.

Neither side said anything about it at the time. Each simply formed an impression of the other and carried it into the next meeting.

The clients' reading had a further cost: it turned a difference of style into a doubt about the contract. Once one client wondered aloud whether Mikko was unhappy, others began watching him for signs of trouble, and found them in every pause.
moreCases.betterRead:
Elfenbein's dialect theory fits this case closely: both sides shared the core meaning of a smile, but used it at very different rates and for different purposes. Neither dialect is wrong. The repair was for both sides to learn a little of the other's. Jess briefed the next clients that Mikko was a quiet, thoughtful man who listened hard. Mikko, without trying to become someone else, made a habit of a smile and a handshake at the start and end of meetings, and of saying aloud, after a long silence, that he was thinking about what they had said. His next three meetings went well. A man does not need to abandon his dialect. He needs to know that it is one.

The lesson runs both ways. Mikko's clients were not shallow for wanting smiles, and Mikko was not cold for withholding them. Each side was using a perfectly good dialect, and each needed a translator until they had learned a little of the other's. A colleague who can explain one side to the other is worth more than any guide to national character.

moreCases.title: Reading his mother-in-law
moreCases.scene:
James, a British accountant, marries Priya, whose family came to Britain from Gujarat. In the first year of their marriage, James finds his
  mother-in-law, Meena, impossible to read. When he offers to help in the kitchen she smiles and tilts her head from side to side, and he cannot
  tell whether she means yes or no. When he says something she disagrees with, she does not argue; she goes quiet and starts serving food. When she is
  pleased with him, she says almost nothing to him directly, but tells Priya on the phone the next day.

  James starts to feel that Meena does not like him, and becomes stiff and formal around her. Priya notices, and is upset that her husband and
  her mother seem to be drifting apart.

Priya, for her part, had never thought to explain her mother's habits, because to her they were simply how her mother was. It took James's growing stiffness for her to see that he was reading a language she had never had to translate.

The visits become tense. James starts finding reasons to arrive late and leave early, and he spends much of each visit in the garden with Priya's father, who talks about cricket and seems easier to understand. Meena, who notices everything, asks Priya whether James is unhappy in the marriage. Priya, caught between them, tells each of them that the other is fine, which is true and which helps nobody. By the end of the first year, James has decided that his mother-in-law simply disapproves of him, and that there is nothing to be done about it.
moreCases.misread:
James read Meena through his own family's dialect, in which approval is usually said to your face, disagreement is argued out, and a side-to-side movement of the head means no. Every signal she sent was translated into the nearest thing in his language, and most of the translations came out cold.

He also never asked. It did not occur to him that the signals might mean something different, because they looked so like signals he already knew.

Each translation also confirmed the one before. Once James suspected that Meena disliked him, her quiet became coldness, her head tilt became refusal, and her silence about his good news became indifference. A first reading, made in the wrong dialect, quietly organised all the later ones.
moreCases.betterRead:
Many of Meena's signals carry different meanings in her dialect. A side-to-side tilt of the head often means yes, or I am listening; quiet rather than argument can be a way of keeping harmony with a son-in-law who is still, in a sense, a guest; and praise passed through a daughter can be a sign of respect rather than distance. James needed an informant, and he had the best possible one beside him. When Priya explained her mother's habits, James began to read her differently, and to ask Priya, after visits, what she thought her mother had meant. Within a year, he could read Meena's head tilt as easily as his own mother's frown.

James also learned to check the readings that mattered most. When he was unsure whether Meena wanted help, he offered in a way that made it easy to decline, and watched what she did rather than what her head did. When she went quiet after a disagreement, he let the subject drop and raised it later with Priya.

workedReading.title: The face in the new office
workedReading.scene:
Six weeks into a new job at a firm's office in Manila, Dan, who has moved from Manchester, announces in a team meeting that a large client has asked for the project to be delivered a month early. Several faces change at once. One colleague, Ria, raises her eyebrows high, widens her eyes and presses her lips together, then smiles. Another, Joel, laughs briefly and looks down at his notes. A third sits completely still. Nobody says anything for a moment, then Ria says, "Okay, sir, we can do it."

Dan likes his team and believes the meeting went well. He has not yet learned how the team usually responds to bad news, because there has not been any until now.

Dan has read about cultural dialects of expression and knows, in theory, that his instincts may not travel. This is the first time he has had to act on that knowledge with something important at stake. The client wants an answer by the end of the week, and whatever he tells them will be hard to take back. He also knows that the answer he heard in the meeting is the one he would most like to believe.

steps.label: Describe before interpreting
steps.text:
Dan has learned to describe movements before he names feelings, and he does it now. Ria: brows raised high, eyes widened, lips pressed, then a smile. Joel: a short laugh, eyes down. The third colleague: no visible movement. Words: agreement from Ria, nothing from anyone else. He notes all of this without deciding what any of it means.

Describing the third colleague's stillness as "no visible movement" is important. It is tempting to call it shock, but stillness is the absence of a signal, not a signal.

He also notes timing. Ria's brows rose first and the smile came after, about a second later. A sequence like that, a strong first movement followed by a social one, is often worth more attention than either movement on its own.

steps.label: Mark the situation
steps.text:
The situation is a manager announcing an unwelcome change to a team in a meeting. In many cultures, including the one he has grown up in, that is a moment when people manage their faces carefully, and in many workplaces in the Philippines, as his colleagues have told him, it can be hard to say no to a manager directly, especially in public.

He also notes that he is the new manager, from abroad, and senior. That position changes what people will feel able to show him, in any culture.

He also notes that a meeting is a public setting. Whatever people feel, they will show less of it here than over coffee afterwards, and in a workplace that prizes smooth relations, the gap between the two may be wide.

steps.label: Check against your dialect
steps.text:
In Dan's own dialect, Ria's raised brows and widened eyes would read as surprise or alarm, the laugh as nervousness, the stillness as shock, and the "we can do it" as agreement. He notes that these are readings in his dialect, not necessarily in theirs. The raised eyebrows in particular may carry other meanings here: he has seen colleagues raise their eyebrows to say yes.

This step is uncomfortable, because it means admitting that his instincts, which have served him for years, may be giving him wrong answers here.

He reminds himself, too, that this is only his sixth week. He has a small sample of how these particular people react to anything, so even a reading that fitted his own dialect would rest on a thin baseline.

steps.label: Hold several readings
steps.text:
The team may be genuinely confident. They may be alarmed and unwilling to say so in a meeting. Ria's "we can do it" may be a commitment, or a polite acknowledgement that the news has been heard, or a way of protecting the team leader's face in front of the new manager. Joel's laugh may be embarrassment or a way of softening the moment. None of these can be settled from faces in an unfamiliar dialect.

Holding the readings open also stops him from acting on the reassuring one, "we can do it", which is the reading he would most like to be true.

Writing the readings down, even briefly, helps him resist the pull of the most comfortable one. On paper, "we can do it" sits next to "we are worried and cannot say so", and both look equally possible.

steps.label: Ask an informant
steps.text:
After the meeting, Dan asks Liza, a senior colleague who has worked with both British and Filipino teams, how she read the room. Liza tells him that a quick yes in a meeting after an unwelcome announcement is often a way of keeping things smooth, and that the real answer usually comes later, in smaller conversations. She suggests he talk to Ria alone.

A good informant is someone who knows both dialects, who is not directly involved, and who will be honest with him. Liza is all three.

He chooses Liza partly because she is not on the project, so her reading will not be coloured by worry about the deadline.

steps.label: Make it safe to answer honestly
steps.text:
Dan finds Ria later and asks her, in private, what she really thinks the team can deliver, and adds that he would rather know now than in three weeks. He makes it clear that saying it is not possible will not count against her.

Asking privately, with an explicit promise that the honest answer is welcome, matters more than any other step. It changes the setting from one in which agreement is expected to one in which the truth is safe.

He also chooses the moment: not straight after the meeting, when Ria might feel she is being checked on, but later in the afternoon, when he can ask about the plan rather than about her reaction.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Ria tells him that the deadline is possible only if two features are dropped, and that the team had been worried but did not want to say no to him in front of everyone. Dan goes back to the client with a revised scope. He notes, for himself, that his reading of the faces had been roughly right about the feeling and completely wrong about what the words meant, and that the informant and the private question had done what no amount of watching could.

He also changes how he will announce bad news in future: briefly in the meeting, followed by short private conversations with each team leader, so that honest answers have somewhere to go.

moreFailures.title: Turning a dialect into a stereotype
moreFailures.body:
Once readers learn that cultures have dialects of expression, they often start applying them to individuals: Koreans hide confusion, Finns never smile, Japanese laugh when embarrassed. These are tendencies, sometimes real ones, and they vary enormously within every culture by age, region, generation, class, temperament and how long someone has lived elsewhere. Part V's chapter on cultural variance describes research showing that differences within countries are far larger than the differences between them. Use what you know about a culture's dialect as a first hypothesis about a person, and then let the person correct you. A Finnish engineer who smiles constantly is not doing Finnishness wrong.

It also helps to notice how you would feel about the reverse: being told, on the strength of your nationality, what your face must mean.

A useful test is to ask whether you would accept the same generalisation about your own group. If a colleague told you that people from your country never show their feelings, you would probably think of a dozen exceptions straight away, starting with yourself. Extend the same courtesy to everyone else.

moreFailures.title: Believing your own face is neutral
moreFailures.body:
Most people experience their own expressions as natural and obvious, and other people's as foreign or hard to read. But your face speaks a dialect too. The amount you smile, the way you show disagreement, how long you hold a silence, whether you nod while listening, how readily you laugh at your own mistakes: all of these were learned, and all of them may be misread by people who learned differently. When you work or live across cultures, it helps to ask someone you trust how your face reads to people there, and to explain your habits aloud where they might cause confusion, as Mikko learned to do.

Even within one country, families, regions and professions have their own dialects. A man who marries into a different family, or moves from a trade to an office, may find his face misread as much as if he had moved abroad.

Video can help here. Watching a recording of yourself in a meeting with the sound off, as Part VI suggests, often shows habits that feel invisible from the inside: a frown of concentration, a flat face while listening, a laugh that arrives at odd moments.

moreFailures.title: Leaning on the face when other channels travel better
moreFailures.body:
The evidence in this chapter suggests that faces are among the least reliable channels across cultures, especially for fine distinctions. Voices, particularly laughter and crying, seem to travel somewhat better, and situations travel best of all: a funeral is a funeral almost everywhere. When you are reading people from an unfamiliar culture, weigh the face least. Pay more attention to the situation, to what people do rather than how they look, to the voice, and to what they say. Halima's face told Tom nothing; her untouched food and her grip on the rail told him a great deal.

The same applies within your own culture when you are reading someone very different from you in age, class or background. The further the dialect from yours, the less weight the face can carry.

None of this means faces are useless across cultures. Broad feelings in strong moments, such as grief at a funeral or joy at a wedding, are usually readable anywhere. The trouble lies in fine distinctions and in the managed, everyday faces of work and polite company, which are exactly the faces most readers spend their time on.

moreFailures.title: Withdrawing because you cannot read anyone
moreFailures.body:
The opposite failure to overconfidence is giving up. People who move to a new country, or work with colleagues from very different backgrounds, sometimes find that their usual readings fail so often that they stop trying, and withdraw into their own group or into a polite, guarded formality. It feels safer, and it is lonely, and it gives everyone less information. The answer is not to stop reading but to read more humbly: to hold readings loosely, to ask informants, to ask people directly when it matters, and to accept that the first year in a new dialect is like the first year in a new language. You will make mistakes. Most people will forgive them, especially if they can see you trying.

It helps to remember that people from the other culture are usually reading you as well, and making their own mistakes. Saying so, lightly, can be a relief to everyone.

Withdrawal also has a quieter version: staying physically present but no longer reading, and treating every face as a blank. That can look like calm, and it is really a kind of absence. People notice when they are no longer being seen.

questions.a:
Smiling in pleasant and sociable situations seems to be found everywhere, and it is among the most reliably recognised expressions across cultures. But what a smile means, when it is expected and how often people use it vary a great deal. In some places people smile at strangers constantly; in others, smiling at a stranger without reason seems odd or insincere. Smiles also do many jobs besides showing pleasure: apologising, appeasing, hiding embarrassment, softening a refusal. Part V's chapter on cultural variance describes research suggesting that in some cultures a smiling face is even judged less intelligent or less honest. Trust a smile a little, everywhere, and its meaning only once you know the dialect.

A useful habit across cultures is to treat a smile as an invitation to keep talking rather than as a statement about how someone feels.

If you come from a culture of frequent smiling and work somewhere it is rarer, it helps to know that a straight face there is often just a resting face, not a verdict on you.

questions.q: Can I learn to read another culture's expressions?
questions.a:
Yes, and you do so the way you learn a language: through exposure, mistakes and informants. Hillary Anger Elfenbein and Nalini Ambady combined many studies of emotion recognition across cultures and found an in-group advantage: people recognise emotions more accurately in members of their own cultural group. They also found that the advantage shrank where groups had more contact with each other. So time helps. Living, working and talking with people from another culture gradually teaches you their dialect, especially if you ask about what you see. The process usually takes months, not days, and it never quite finishes.

Films, television and novels from another culture help too, though they show heightened versions of everyday expression. Ordinary conversation is the real classroom.

Reading about a culture can help as a starting point, but it works best as a list of questions to ask rather than answers to rely on. A guidebook that says people in a country avoid saying no directly tells you to listen for indirect refusals; it cannot tell you how a particular colleague refuses.

questions.q: What does the study of six million videos actually show?
questions.a:
Cowen, Keltner and colleagues used machine learning to find about sixteen kinds of facial expression in millions of videos from 144 countries, and found that each kind tended to appear in similar kinds of situation in every region they studied, with the pattern of context links about seventy percent preserved across regions. That is strong evidence that similar faces turn up in similar situations worldwide. It is weaker evidence about what people feel, because the study measured faces and situations, not feelings, and because the algorithm was trained on human judgments that may carry their own cultural assumptions. Lisa Feldman Barrett, commenting on the study, praised its use of real-world settings while raising exactly that question.

For a reader, the practical message is modest: similar situations seem to produce broadly similar faces in many places, which is useful, and a face still needs its situation, its person and often a question before it means anything.

It is also worth knowing what the study did not look at: what people said they felt, or how faces varied between individuals within each region. Those are exactly the questions a reader in a real conversation needs answered, which is why the study supports a broad picture rather than a method for reading individuals.

questions.q: Do people always read their own culture better?
questions.a:
On average, yes, a little, which is what the in-group advantage describes. But the advantage is modest, it varies a great deal between individuals and emotions, and it shrinks with contact. Some people are better at reading strangers from other cultures than many people are at reading their own families. And within any culture, people misread each other constantly, which is why this book's methods, baseline, cluster, context and asking, apply at home as much as abroad.

It is also worth remembering that "your own culture" is not a single thing. A Londoner and a Glaswegian, or a farmer and a barrister, may read each other with as much difficulty as people from different countries.

Many people who have lived abroad for years describe a related experience: they come to read their adopted culture well and, on returning home, feel briefly out of step with their own. Dialects can be learned, and they also need practice to stay fluent.

questions.q: What should I do when I cannot read anyone around me?
questions.a:
Slow down and rely more on words. Say more out loud than you would at home: that you are pleased, that you are thinking, that you would like to know what someone really thinks. Ask more questions, privately, and make it safe for people to give honest answers. Find an informant, someone who knows both your dialect and theirs, and ask them how a meeting read. Watch how local people respond to each other, which is often more revealing than how they respond to you. And remember that the people around you may be finding you just as hard to read.

It can also help to tell people that you are new and still learning how things work. Most people respond to that with patience, and some with very useful explanations.

It also helps to keep a short note of the readings you get wrong and what the right answer turned out to be. Over a few months, the notes become a personal dictionary of the new dialect, and the same mistakes start to repeat less often.

questions.q: Are gestures part of this debate?
questions.a:
Not in the same way. Facial expressions are argued about because they might be biologically shared. Most gestures, such as the thumbs-up, the ring, beckoning or pointing, are clearly learned conventions, and they vary across cultures in ways that can be mapped. Part V's chapter on cultural variance gives that map, along with its limits. Head movements for yes and no fall somewhere between the two, and Part III's chapter on the head nod covers them. The working rule is the same for all of them: what feels natural to you is a habit, and someone else's habit may be different.

Gestures can also be learned deliberately, from a guide or an informant, far more easily than facial dialects, because they are more conscious and more often explained.

One practical point: if you are unsure of a gesture, do less of it. An open hand and a clear spoken word are rarely misread; a hand sign that is friendly at home may be rude elsewhere.

watch.title: Lost in Translation: Official Trailer
watch.notice: An American actor adrift in Tokyo. Watch the bows, the baffling translations and the small mismatches of gesture and timing that leave him on the outside of every exchange.

reviewPrompt: The next time you read an unfamiliar face, describe the movement and the situation, and ask before trusting any fine distinction.
